chapters.title: Two kinds of move, one number
chapters.dek: A stock's variance between now and expiry has an ordinary part that accumulates smoothly and a scheduled part that arrives all at once.

figures.title: Variance accumulating toward expiry
figures.caption: Drag the event date and watch the step slide along the ramp. The lower panel is the number actually on your screen: it jumps the moment the event enters the window, then decays as the diffusive term catches up. Nothing about the stock changed — only how much time the same lump is being spread over.

checks.q: A name has 25% diffusive vol and an earnings event worth a 6% move. Why is the two-week implied vol so much higher than the two-month?
checks.right: Both windows contain the same event variance J², but the front spreads it over about a quarter of the time — 14 days against 60 — so J²/T is about four times larger
checks.why: Same lump, less time. The event contributes a fixed J² to both windows. Quoted vol is √(total variance / T), so dividing that fixed contribution by a smaller T inflates the front-month number without anything about the event being different. This is why comparing front and back implied vols on an earnings name tells you almost nothing until you strip the event out — which is chapter 03.

chapters.text: Page 01 modeled a stock as pure diffusion — many small independent moves, variance accruing evenly with time. That is a decent description of most days and a terrible description of the morning after an earnings release, when the whole distribution of a quarter's worth of information resolves in a single print. The fix is not a more complicated process. It is to admit there are two sources of variance and to add them, which you are allowed to do because variance is additive over independent components — the same fact page 01 used to derive √T scaling, applied along a different seam. [equation: σ_imp² · T = σ_diff² · T + J²] Reads as: total variance is the ordinary variance that accumulates with time, plus a fixed lump the event contributes regardless of how far away it is. Look carefully at the asymmetry in that equation, because everything downstream comes from it. The diffusive term is multiplied by T — the longer the window, the more of it you accumulate. The event term is not . A single earnings release contributes the same J² whether it sits inside a one-week option or a one-year option. Which immediately explains the shape of every earnings term structure you have ever seen. Divide through by T to get the quoted volatility, and the event's contribution is J²/T — enormous in the front month and negligible in the back. The front is not "expensive." It is carrying the same lump of event variance over far less time. The figure shows the two components accumulating. Diffusion is the ramp; the event is the step. What the market quotes is neither — it is the square root of their sum, divided by elapsed time. chapters.title: Not all days are equal
chapters.dek: Calendar time is a poor clock for volatility. Desks replace it with a weighted one, and the weights are a view.

figures.title: The weights
figures.caption: The step is the whole point. A term structure built from weighted days has a discontinuity exactly at the event, and the size of the step is a direct readout of what the market thinks the event is worth. Reading that step is the next chapter.

chapters.text: Black–Scholes accrues variance uniformly in calendar time, which implies a weekend contains as much risk as a Wednesday. It does not. Markets are shut, and while some information still arrives, empirically a weekend behaves like a fraction of a trading day rather than two full ones. The practical fix is to stop using calendar days as the clock and start assigning each day a weight : how much variance it contributes relative to an ordinary trading day. An ordinary day is 1.0. A weekend day is perhaps 0.1 to 0.2. A holiday is low. The day after a long weekend is often slightly above 1. And an earnings day is three to five , because a quarter's information lands in one session. [equation: total variance = σ_ref² × ( Σ w_i ) / 252] Reads as: add up the weights of the days you actually hold the option, not the days on the calendar. σ_ref is the vol of a single ordinary day, annualized. Editing the weights below is the closest thing on this page to what a vol desk actually does before an earnings season. The term structure it produces is not fitted to anything — it falls out of the weights, and every kink in it is a day you decided was special. Notice what happens as you slide the earnings date. Every expiry before the event is unaffected; every expiry after it jumps. With the event on day 21 and a weight of 4, the twenty-day implied vol is 25.97% and the twenty-one-day is 28.54% — a 2.6-point step from one expiry to the next, caused entirely by a single day crossing into the window. The weights Each bar is one calendar day's contribution relative to an ordinary trading day. The term structure those weights imply Calendar The step is the whole point. A term structure built from weighted days has a discontinuity exactly at the event, and the size of the step is a direct readout of what the market thinks the event is worth. Reading that step is the next chapter. Try this Give the earnings day a weight of one — treat it as an ordinary day — and predict what the fair term structure does.

chapters.title: Stripping the event out
chapters.dek: Two expiries, two unknowns, one linear solve. The messy curve becomes a flat one and a single number.

figures.title: Before and after the strip
figures.caption: Move the two chosen expiries anywhere on the curve and the recovered numbers barely change — which is the test that the decomposition is describing the data rather than fitting it. When the recovered σ_d starts drifting with your choice of expiries, that is evidence of a second event, or of an event whose date you have wrong.

chapters.text: Take two expiries that both contain the event. Each satisfies the same decomposition with the same two unknowns: [equation: σ₁²T₁ = σ_d²T₁ + J² · σ₂²T₂ = σ_d²T₂ + J²] Reads as: two equations, two unknowns. The event term is identical in both because it is the same event; only the time differs. Subtract them and J² cancels, leaving the diffusive vol directly. Substitute back for J: [equation: σ_d² = (σ₁²T₁ − σ₂²T₂) / (T₁ − T₂) · J = √(σ₁²T₁ − σ_d²T₁)] Reads as: the slope of total variance against time is the diffusive variance; whatever is left over is the event. That is the entire method, and it is exact rather than approximate. A front month at 39.54% and a back month at 29.05% — a wildly inverted, unhelpful-looking pair — recover σ_d = 25.000% and J = 6.000% . The inversion was never a signal about the diffusive vol. It was one number hiding in the curve. The figure is the payoff for the whole page. On the left, the raw term structure: kinked, inverted, apparently telling you something complicated. On the right, the same curve with J² removed from every point. It goes flat. The complexity was one scalar. Before and after the strip Recovered from any two expiries you pick Market Move the two chosen expiries anywhere on the curve and the recovered numbers barely change — which is the test that the decomposition is describing the data rather than fitting it. When the recovered σ_d starts drifting with your choice of expiries, that is evidence of a second event, or of an event whose date you have wrong. Try this Move the two expiries closer together and predict whether the solve gets more or less stable. Derivation — why the event term does not scale with time Split the log return to expiry into two independent pieces: the accumulated diffusion, and the jump that occurs if the event falls inside the window. [equation: ln(S_T/S₀) = X_diff + X_event] Reads as: the total move is ordinary drift plus, once, the shock. Independence means variances add with no cross term: [equation: Var(total) = Var(X_diff) + Var(X_event) = σ_d²T + J²] Reads as: independent risks add in variance, so the two pieces simply stack. No cross term, because the event does not know what the diffusion did. The diffusion is a sum of T years' worth of independent increments, so its variance is proportional to T. The event is a single draw. It happens once, and its variance is whatever it is, regardless of how much time surrounds it. That is the entire asymmetry, and everything on this page is a consequence of it. Divide by T to get quoted volatility and the two terms behave completely differently: [equation: σ_imp² = σ_d² + J²/T] Reads as: quoted variance is the diffusive level plus an event term that decays like 1/T. Plot this against 1/T and it is a straight line whose intercept is σ_d² and whose slope is J². That linearization is worth knowing as a practical trick: plot quoted variance against 1/T across every expiry, and if the points fall on a line, one event explains the whole curve. Curvature means more than one thing is going on. Where it breaks. Two events in one window give you two lumps that cannot be separated from two expiries alone — you need a third, and you need to know the dates. Vol also leaks: the market often bids the event premium up in the days before the print, so J measured a week out is not J measured the morning of. And an event whose date is not yet confirmed smears the lump across several possible days, which flattens the step and biases J downward.

chapters.title: The implied move, and the factor everyone drops
chapters.dek: The number quoted on every earnings preview is not a standard deviation. It is about 80% of one.

figures.title: Two different "expected moves" on the same distribution
figures.caption: The shaded region is where the move exceeds the straddle-implied number. It is 42% of the distribution — far more than the 32% a one-sigma band would leave outside, which surprises people who have been treating that number as one. The ratio between the two markers is always √(2/π) — it does not depend on volatility, spot or tenor.

checks.q: An earnings preview says "the options are implying a 7% move." The stock moves 8%. Was the market wrong?
checks.right: Not necessarily. That number is an average, not a threshold — about 42% of moves exceed it, so an 8% print against a 7% implied is an ordinary outcome
checks.why: A single move above the implied move says almost nothing. The straddle price is the mean absolute move, and the distribution of absolute moves is right-skewed: the majority of outcomes — about 58% — land below the mean, while a minority of large ones pull the average up to it. So roughly 42% of moves exceed the implied move, against 32% for a genuine one-sigma move. Being wrong would require the average of many such prints to miss, not one of them. Judging an implied move from one print is like judging a coin from one flip — and note the second answer's caveat, because a straddle buyer can still lose on an 8% move if the vol crush costs more than the gamma gained, which is chapter 05.

terms.Implied move: The size of the move the option market is pricing for an event. Usually quoted from the straddle, which makes it an expected absolute move rather than a standard deviation.
terms.Straddle: A call and a put at the same strike. Its price is the market's expected absolute move, which is a smaller number than one standard deviation and gets confused with it constantly.
terms.Vol crush: The collapse in implied volatility immediately after a scheduled event. Not a mispricing correcting — the event variance has simply been used up and is no longer in the remaining life.

chapters.text: Having recovered J, converting it to dollars looks trivial — multiply by spot. But the number the market quotes as the implied move is usually derived from the straddle price, and that is a different quantity from a one-standard-deviation move. The gap is large and it is a constant, so it is worth getting right once. Here is the fact. For a driftless lognormal, the price of an at-the-money straddle equals the expected absolute move : [equation: Straddle = E |S_T − S₀| = √(2/π) · S · σ√T ≈ 0.7979 · S · σ√T] Reads as: a straddle costs exactly the average size of the move, ignoring direction. Which makes sense — that is what it pays. A one-standard-deviation move is S·σ√T , with no 0.7979 in front. So the straddle-derived implied move is about 80% of a one-sigma move , and the two get used interchangeably all the time. At 20 vol over 30 days on a $100 stock the straddle is 4.57 while one sigma is 5.73 — a 25% difference in a number people quote to two decimals. The consequence is concrete. If you read "the options imply a 4.6% move" and then reason about the probability of exceeding it as though it were a standard deviation, you will overstate how unusual a larger move is. For a lognormal, the stock exceeds the straddle-implied move about 42% of the time, and exceeds a genuine one-sigma move about 32% of the time. Both are printed live in the panel beside the figure, and they are very different claims. It is 42% of the distribution — far more than the 32% a one-sigma band would leave outside, which surprises people who have been treating that number as one. The ratio between the two markers is always √(2/π) — it does not depend on volatility, spot or tenor.

chapters.title: Through the print
chapters.dek: A fairly priced earnings straddle loses money about two times in three. That is not a mispricing — it is the shape of the payoff.

figures.title: P&L of a long earnings straddle, held through the print
figures.caption: Set realized equal to implied and read the two statistics against each other: a mean at zero and a median well below it. That gap is the trade. Everything about how event vol feels to trade — and most of the behavioral errors around it — comes from the distance between those two numbers.

figures.title: Trade the print
figures.caption: The first report prices a 10.8% move; the stock moves half a percent and ten long straddles lose $4,729 to the vol crush. Over 2,000 reports, buying every straddle wins only 30.8% of the time and still comes out close to even, $58 a report: the big prints pay for the many small ones. Buying when the last four prints averaged more than 1.2 times implied and selling when they averaged under 0.8 makes $694 a report and wins 63% of its trades.

checks.q: You have bought fairly priced earnings straddles eight times and lost on six. What does that tell you?
checks.right: Almost nothing — a 33% win rate is the expected shape of a fairly priced long-vol event trade, and eight trades cannot distinguish fair from unfair
checks.why: Six losses in eight is the base case. At a fair price the win rate is about a third, so losing six of eight is close to the mode of the outcome distribution and carries almost no information about whether you are being charged too much. Judging this strategy needs the sum of P&L over a large sample, not the hit rate — and the sample has to be large because the payoff is dominated by rare large wins. The fourth answer is the trap: it is exactly the inference that a 67% loss rate invites, and it puts you short a tail you have just watched not happen.

chapters.text: Buy the straddle the afternoon before the print, sell it the morning after. Two things happen overnight and they pull against each other. The stock gaps, which helps you. And the implied volatility collapses , because J has left the window — every remaining day is now an ordinary day, and the option reprices at σ_diff instead of σ_imp. That is the vol crush, and it is not a market overreaction. It is the arithmetic of chapter 01 running in reverse. Simulate it a few thousand times with realized event vol set exactly equal to implied — a perfectly fair price, by construction — and look at the distribution. The mean is about zero — −0.07, which is the single day of ordinary theta you pay for holding the position overnight, and the residual is what "fairly priced" leaves behind. The median is around −0.94 , and the win rate is 33% . You lose, modestly, in two trades out of three, and the trade is nonetheless fairly priced, because the third outcome is large enough to pay for the other two. This is the single most important thing to understand about event vol, and it is a psychological problem more than a mathematical one. A strategy that loses two thirds of the time feels broken long before the sample is large enough to say anything. Traders abandon fairly priced long-vol event trades constantly, and buy fairly priced short-vol event trades enthusiastically, because a 67% win rate feels like skill until the fourth trade. Push realized above implied and the whole distribution shifts right — at 1.5× implied the win rate goes to 52% and the mean to +1.67. Push it below and the picture is brutal: at half implied you win 5% of the time. The asymmetry between those two cases is why selling event vol looks so attractive and why it periodically ends careers. That gap is the trade. Everything about how event vol feels to trade — and most of the behavioral errors around it — comes from the distance between those two numbers. Try this Set your view of the event equal to the market's and predict whether the P&L distribution becomes symmetric. Knowing the shape is one thing; living through it is another. Trade a season of reports. Each round is a company reporting tomorrow, its straddle priced off the implied move, and the one clue a desk actually uses: how big this company's last four prints were compared with what was implied going in. Buy, sell or pass ten straddles, then watch the print and the vol crush. Trade the print Your straddles The first report prices a 10.8% move; the stock moves half a percent and ten long straddles lose $4,729 to the vol crush. Over 2,000 reports, buying every straddle wins only 30.8% of the time and still comes out close to even, $58 a report: the big prints pay for the many small ones. Buying when the last four prints averaged more than 1.2 times implied and selling when they averaged under 0.8 makes $694 a report and wins 63% of its trades. Trader's lens An event-vol trader does not ask whether the stock will move; it will. They ask whether it will move more than the straddle says, and the best evidence is this company's own history of prints against what was implied. A long straddle into earnings is a bet that loses most nights and is sized so the nights it wins pay for the rest. Compare implied moves with realized ones company by company; the ratio is sticky. The vol crush is certain; the move is not. Long straddles pay for the crush every time. Short straddles win most prints and lose big on the few that gap. Size them for the gap. Rule of thumb: the implied move ≈ straddle ÷ spot; buy it only when this name's prints have run above it.

chapters.title: Expressing it
chapters.dek: If your view is about the event rather than the stock, the front month alone is the wrong instrument.

figures.title: Where your view actually shows up
figures.caption: The lower panel is the shape that matters: your disagreement is concentrated almost entirely in the front and decays like 1/T. That concentration is what makes calendars the natural vehicle, and it is also why a view on an event is worth very little expressed in a one-year option.

chapters.text: Suppose the strip says the market is charging J = 6% for a print and you think it is worth 4%. Buying or selling the front month expresses that, but it expresses a great deal else besides — you are also taking a position in the diffusive vol, and in the direction, and in the gamma between now and expiry. The cleaner expression is a calendar : trade the front month against the back. Because both expiries share the same σ_d and only the front carries a meaningful J²/T, the spread isolates the event. Sell the front and buy the back and you are short the event and roughly flat the diffusive level. The numbers make the case. On a name with 25% diffusive vol and a 6% event, a two-week option prices at 39.5% and a two-month at 29.1%. If you think J is really 4%, the fair front-month vol is 32.3% — a 7.3-point difference in the front against 2.2 points at two months. Nearly all of your edge is in the near expiry, and nearly all of the risk you did not want is in the shared diffusive component that the spread cancels. Two warnings, both from chapter 01's asymmetry. First, a calendar is not a clean event bet: the legs have different gammas and different vegas, so you are still short front gamma when you sell the front, and a large move hurts you regardless of what the vol does. Second, the event has to actually happen inside the front expiry — a confirmed date matters more than the vol level, and a date that moves turns the position into something you did not choose. chapters.title: Event drill
chapters.dek: Stripping, implied moves, and the conversions that get fumbled under time pressure.
chapters.text: The arithmetic of event vol is variance arithmetic, which means the mistakes are always the same two: averaging volatilities instead of variances, and treating a straddle-implied move as a standard deviation. Both are drilled here. Tolerance is ±1% on Core and ±0.5% on Full. Correct 0 / 0 Streak 0 Best 0 Difficulty Core Full Question Loading… Check Skip

chapters.title: Check yourself

checks.q: Why does variance get added rather than volatility?
checks.right: Because variance is what accumulates along a path. Independent sources of movement add their squared contributions, so σ²T = σ_diff²·T + ΣJ² and volatilities do not add at all
checks.why: Variance is the additive quantity. That single fact is the whole page — it is what makes a two-expiry solve possible and what makes a kinked term structure go flat once one number is removed.

checks.q: Two expiries, one event between them. What can you recover?
checks.right: Both the diffusive volatility and the event's size, exactly. A 39.54% front and 29.05% back recover σ_diff = 25.000% and J = 6.000% from any pair
checks.why: Both, exactly. Two equations, two unknowns, and the equations are exact because variance is additive. The solve works from any pair of expiries that bracket the event.

checks.q: At 20 volatility with 30 days to run, the straddle is 4.57 and one standard deviation is 5.73. Why the gap?
checks.right: They are different quantities. A straddle prices the expected absolute move, which is √(2/π) ≈ 0.7979 of a standard deviation — a 25% gap in a number quoted to two decimals
checks.why: Expected absolute move versus standard deviation. The 0.8 in the rule of thumb is √(2/π), and treating the implied move as a one-sigma number overstates the odds of staying inside it every single time.

checks.q: A fairly priced earnings straddle. What does its P&L distribution look like?
checks.right: Mean about zero, median about −0.94, and a win rate near 33%. Mostly small losses with occasional large wins
checks.why: Mean zero, median negative, wins one time in three. The gap between mean and median is the whole behavioral problem with event volatility: a correctly priced trade feels wrong two-thirds of the time.

checks.q: Why weight days rather than count them?
checks.right: Because days contribute unequally to variance. Weekends contribute almost nothing and an earnings day contributes three or four ordinary days' worth, so calendar time is the wrong clock
checks.why: Days are not interchangeable units of variance. Once you weight them the fair term structure falls straight out, and a curve that looked strangely kinked turns out to be exactly right.

checks.q: Why is a calendar the natural expression of an event view?
checks.right: Because the trade is about the front-versus-back relationship, which is precisely what the event creates. The calendar isolates the term-structure difference the event is responsible for
checks.why: The event lives in the front-back relationship. An outright straddle mixes the event with the diffusive volatility around it; the calendar is the structure that asks the question the analysis actually answered.
